phase: The BarberOS audit results are readable in production. Migration 0055 was applied on 2026-09-17 under CEO approval -- individually, because the drift blocks the batch path -- and verified afterwards by fingerprint against a local build from empty, with security advisors unchanged and the data untouched. Reading the 40 runs immediately earned its keep by exposing two errors of mine, both caught by the fingerprint rather than by reading the code: I had dropped in-body comments by retyping the SQL for the apply, and I had asserted a production number ('0 of 3 dimensions') invented from my own test fixture. Both repaired forward and corrected everywhere they had spread. What the runs say is now visible and uncomfortable: 40 sales hooks, and not one of the 45 findings behind them carries any evidence. That is the next decision and it is a business one. The product's other gaps are unchanged: the client book is empty, the only shop is a test shop with an unpublished page, no BarberOS application exists in this repository, and nothing is deployed or has egress.

Video Studio: a still image becomes a video, from inside the console. @hl-bos/video-studio finds the panels in a composite image by scoring every row and column for uniformity (a gutter is uniform along its length, artwork is not), plans a shot list of pans and zooms, and resolves that plan to exact rectangles at any millisecond; the Control Center's /video page records it to a real .mp4 in the browser with no account, no key and no upload. Verified end to end in headless Chromium against the CEO's own six-panel image: 6 panels found in a 3x2 grid, 8 shots, 16.7s, 1440x1416 MP4 of 7.3 MB that decodes and contains real frames. 62 unit tests. One real defect was found and fixed by that verification: the first cut cropped near-square comic panels to 16:9 and deleted the artist's caption bars, and the fix (contain-by-default framing) exposed a second bug where the renderer stretched instead of padding -- both now have regression tests that fail without the fix. Generated motion (a video model that animates the picture) is NOT built: the page names it, says what it would take, and shows no button for it.

Video Studio, second pass: the page told the CEO that generated motion needs a paid account, which is false and false in the expensive direction. Corrected: the provider panel now names the route that is genuinely our own (a freely licensed open model -- Wan, LTX -- on hardware we own, nothing metered, no image leaving our systems), states what every route costs in words about money, and is ordered cheapest-first. Status renamed needs-account -> not-built, because what is missing is the connection code, not the money. The console also now answers 'do I have an NVIDIA card?' itself, on the Video Studio page, rather than sending anyone to Device Manager -- it runs nvidia-smi, falls back to the Windows display-adapter list, distinguishes 'no card' from 'card with a missing driver', maps video memory to which models are actually runnable, and shows what it ran. The Windows branch cannot execute on the machine this was written on, so the whole decision is injectable and proved by five injected-probe tests; a mutation check confirmed they fail without the platform guard. Also fixed two shipped rendering defects found by reading the served HTML rather than the source: a sentence template that spliced a provider name into nonsense, and this toolchain dropping the space after a closing inline tag, which shipped the word 'notautomatically'.

The console can now RECEIVE work, not just send it. Until now the launcher could start the console but never update it, so once a copy of this repository was on the CEO's machine there was no way for finished work to reach him short of typing git commands -- the exact chore the operating contract forbids, and a hole left by every previous session including the one that wrote the launcher. scripts/update.mjs now runs on every start: it collects whatever has been finished since last time, reinstalls libraries if they changed, rebuilds if the code changed, then starts. It never destroys work (a folder with unsaved changes is left alone), never rewrites history (fast-forward only; a diverged folder stops and says so), never blocks startup (no network means one line and carry on), and never hangs on a credential prompt (GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, so a private repo fails in seconds instead of freezing the launcher). Proved by scripts/local-test/verify-update.sh against real throwaway git repositories -- 7 git cases and 4 launcher-decision cases, all passing. One real batch defect was caught and fixed in the writing: `if A if B (X) else (Y)` binds the else to the inner if, so the first draft would have skipped the build entirely on a fresh clone and started a console that had never been built.

ATS Resume Optimizer: a working career tool, not a demo. @hl-bos/ats-resume parses a master resume and a job posting, builds an evidence matrix of every requirement against the candidate's own words, maps terminology (work stated in the posting's language, with the original detail and every number carried through), scores the fit on the owner's weighting and projects a second score that only counts revisions the evidence supports. apps/ats-resume-optimizer is the seven-screen app over it, with a split-screen review where every generated sentence discloses its source evidence, the requirement it answers and why it is worded that way. DOCX and PDF are generated from scratch (a ZIP/OOXML writer and a base-14 PDF writer, no document dependencies) and both round-trip: the text reads back out of the files we write. The central promise is enforced where the bytes are produced, not in the UI -- proved end to end against the running app by editing a bullet to an invented "$250M P&L across 14 countries", watching the validator name all three fabricated figures, and confirming the export dropped the line (X-Claims-Dropped: 1) while still writing the other eleven. Running it also found four real defects that reading the code had not: posting metadata ("Employment type: Full-time") being scored as an unmet requirement; a terminology rewrite that turned an $18M operating budget into "P&L ownership" (a P&L has a revenue line -- budget adjacency is now reported as a partial match with the difference spelled out); a splice-based rewrite producing broken English ("Cut warehouse and distribution operations, including dock dwell time by 27%"); and a stale-cache bug that served a previously exported document after an edit. Migration 0048 (ats, 17 tables) is written and verified against a local PostgreSQL 16 -- RLS enabled AND forced on all 17, 68 policies, zero anon grants, and the anti-fabrication CHECK constraints exercised -- and is UNAPPLIED to any project. No AI key is required: the built-in rules engine runs every feature, and Claude is an optional enhancement whose every suggestion is re-checked against the same evidence. The console can start it: a "Your software" panel on the Control Center home page shows whether it is running and starts it with one click, building first and waiting for a real health response before it reports success or offers a link -- the operating contract forbids telling the CEO to run a command, so "pnpm dev" was a feature request for the console, not an instruction for him.

BarberOS current-state audit, and the correction that followed. The audit searched this repository against the BarberOS brief and reported that BarberOS did not exist -- no app, package, schema, route or test -- with the word 'barber' appearing only as an industry taxonomy label in five files. That was correct about the repository and WRONG about the product. Reading the live database next showed BarberOS installed and running in canonical production: eleven migrations (0048_barberos_capability_catalog through 0058_barberos_client_crm) that are in no repository file, a barberos schema of 14 tables with RLS enabled and forced, a transform_audit schema of 10, 27 functions in each, and 17 public barberos_* RPCs. Two capabilities the audit had listed as MISSING are in fact built: client_rhythm/clients_due (learns a client's typical haircut interval and ranks who is overdue) and an owned-website builder with a real publish lifecycle. Revised completeness against the brief: about 35 percent, not 20-25, moving the workflow map from 1 EXISTS / 9 PARTIAL / 10 MISSING to 1 / 12 / 7. The honest limits matter as much: the client book is EMPTY (0 clients, 0 visits), the only shop is 'Herman Legacy Test Shop' with an unpublished site, transform_audit has NO public API so its 40 runs and 45 findings cannot be read by anything, and every one of those findings is confidence='inferred' with zero evidence URLs and a composite score of 0 -- the diagnostic has never actually fetched a website, because nothing is deployed and nothing has egress. No BarberOS code exists in this repository, so none of it is tested or reviewable here. Read-only throughout: nothing was created, altered, applied or deleted. docs/products/barberos/01-current-state-audit.md and 02-production-drift-map.md.

BarberOS is in source control. The barberos schema -- 14 tables, 27 functions and the 17 public RPCs that were only ever in production -- is now four migrations (0049-0052) in this repository, with the pgTAP suite it never had: 74 assertions. Four rather than eleven on purpose: the live database records what exists, not which migration created which object, so splitting it to mimic production's history would have been invented history. NOTHING WAS APPLIED -- these reproduce what is already there, and .hlbos/canonical.json records the mapping. Fidelity was proved rather than asserted: a twelve-category structural fingerprint (columns, constraints, indexes, policies, RLS flags, triggers, functions, function grants, table grants, enums, seeded rows, permissions) computed identically against canonical production and against a local PostgreSQL 16.13 with all 52 migrations applied from empty -- all twelve match. That comparison found a real divergence reading the code had not: the first draft dropped a grant production carries. Running the tests found three more of my own errors, all of the same dangerous kind -- assertions that passed while proving nothing. The capability-trigger and constraint tests ran as a signed-in user, where authenticated holds only SELECT, so every one failed on the GRANT with the same 42501 the trigger raises; a prerequisite test used a capability whose prerequisite was already enabled; and a cross-tenant test passed a null id hidden by the other tenant's RLS, so it failed for the wrong reason. A mutation check confirms the suite now bites. Verified in full locally: 983 pgTAP assertions 0 failing (909 before), 860 unit tests, format, lint, typecheck 18/18, migration and lineage checks green at 52. Recorded and NOT fixed: the five trigger functions carry PostgreSQL's default PUBLIC EXECUTE, exactly as production does -- inert, asserted, and worth its own deliberate migration rather than a behaviour change smuggled in under a reconciliation. transform_audit (10 tables, 27 functions, 40 diagnostic runs, 50 prospects) is still only in production; that is next.

The BarberOS diagnostic engine is in source control too. transform_audit -- 10 tables and 27 functions that were only ever in production -- is now migrations 0053-0054 with a 77-assertion pgTAP suite, which closes the reconstruction: all eleven of the out-of-repo BarberOS migrations are now covered by six repo migrations. NOTHING WAS APPLIED. Verified the same way as before, by structural fingerprint against canonical production and against a local PostgreSQL 16.13 with all 54 migrations applied from empty: eleven categories, all matching. And again it caught something reading the code had not -- my draft granted recompute_composite to authenticated, which production deliberately withholds because that is the ONLY function permitted to write the derived score, and granting it directly would have handed a caller exactly what deny_derived_write() exists to prevent. Production was tighter than my reconstruction. What this schema is: the pre-sale diagnostic, agency-tenant scoped -- the tenant is us doing the auditing, not the shop. Campaign weights the dimensions, a run scores one prospect, findings are the evidence, recommendations resolve to real BarberOS capabilities, then the discovery call and the proposal. Its guards are the point, because this is where an overstatement becomes a commercial promise: findings are append-only, 'unknown' and a null score are the same fact, a dimension cannot be called verified without a finding carrying an evidence URL, composite_score is derived and cannot be written by hand, an outreach hook must cite a finding from its own run, a proposal cannot name a capability the catalog lacks or mention a deferred one at all or call a planned one deliverable today, and a sent proposal cannot be edited. One of those explains the production data directly: a weighted dimension only counts as assessed if it is not 'unknown', which is why all 40 real runs read partially_completed and score 0 -- the engine is being honest about never having looked. Running the tests found a real flake of my own: every row in a pgTAP test shares a created_at because now() is transaction time, so an assertion reading position 0 of a created_at-ordered list picked the wrong proposal; it now looks it up by id. Mutation checks confirm the suite bites -- dropping the append-only trigger fails 2 assertions, dropping the proposal-honesty trigger fails 7. Verified in full: 1060 pgTAP assertions 0 failing (983 before), 860 unit tests, format, lint, typecheck 18/18, migration and lineage checks green at 54. STILL OPEN, and now the shortest path to value: transform_audit has no public API at all, so those 40 runs cannot be read by any application.

The BarberOS audit results can be read. transform_audit held 27 functions and, in production, 40 recorded audit runs against 50 real Western New York barbershops -- and nothing could reach a single one of them, because the schema is not exposed through PostgREST and had zero public RPCs. Migration 0055 adds 22 public.barberos_audit_* functions plus the three reads the schema was missing entirely (it could fetch one run by id but had no way to FIND a run, which makes an API useless) and a permission-checked path for recording a competitor, which previously required a direct table write nobody is allowed to make. THIS ONE IS NEW WORK, NOT A RECONSTRUCTION: unlike 0049-0054 it does not exist in production, and it is UNAPPLIED pending your approval. Two design rules are enforced by test rather than trusted. First, a wrapper adds reachability and never authority: every public function is SECURITY INVOKER and delegates to a function that checks its own permission, so the suite drives the entire audit through the public surface and then calls it again as a viewer (read-only), as a role with no audit permission at all, and as another agency -- each refused exactly what the inner function would have refused. A mutation proved it bites: rewriting one wrapper to read the table itself as definer broke the escalation assertion. Second, the score never travels without its coverage -- every response carrying composite_score carries coverage in the same object, because in production every run scores 0 with 0 of 3 dimensions assessed, and a caller must not be able to render '0/100' as a judgement about the barbershop when it is an admission about us. The run list also counts findings and evidenced findings separately, so '45 findings' can never read as '45 evidenced findings'. 55 new assertions. Also fixed a stale assertion of my own: 53_transform_audit.sql claimed the schema had no public API by counting names that the shipped API does not match, so it would have kept passing vacuously forever; it now asserts the real surface. Verified locally: 55 migrations applied from empty, 1115 pgTAP assertions 0 failing (1060 before), 860 unit tests, format, lint, typecheck 18/18, migration and lineage checks green at 55.

Apply migration 0055 (BarberOS Audit public API) to production -- DONE, 2026-09-17 under CEO approval. Applied individually rather than as a batch, because the recorded drift means the protected one-click workflow cannot pass its own check; same approach as 0046/0047. Recorded as version 20260917212122. Verified after: signatures, grants and function bodies all fingerprint-identical to a local PostgreSQL 16.13 with all 55 migrations applied from empty; 22 public functions, none SECURITY DEFINER, none reachable by anon, all with search_path pinned; security advisors unchanged at 40 findings, finding for finding; 40 runs, 45 findings and 40 recommendations untouched. Fail-closed proved in production: an unauthenticated call raises 42501 from the inner function through the wrapper. Two forward-repairs were needed, both my fault and both caught by the fingerprint rather than by reading: 0055r01 restored five in-body comments the first apply dropped because I retyped the SQL instead of sending the committed file (22 of 26 bodies had matched; 4 had not), and 0055r02 corrected a comment asserting 'every run reads 0 of 3 dimensions' -- a number I had invented from my own test fixture. THE 40 RUNS ARE NOW READABLE, and reading them is what exposed that error.

What the 40 audit runs actually say, now that they can be read -- and the decision it forces. The campaign weights ONE dimension (website, 100). 35 runs read completed with coverage 1 of 1 and a composite of 0; 5 read partially_completed at 0 of 1 with no score at all. 50 shops are on file, 40 of them audited. Across all 45 findings, NOT ONE carries an evidence URL. Zero shops have a Google Place ID, Instagram or Facebook link recorded, and zero discovery calls have been logged. And all 40 runs carry an outreach hook. That last pair is what needs your attention: there are 40 sales hooks and none of them rests on evidence. A real one, verbatim from production -- 'There is no website behind your name, so every search that finds you ends there.' The finding it cites is confidence 'inferred' with a null evidence URL, inferred from a blank column in an imported spreadsheet, because nothing has ever looked at that shop. The schema's guard did exactly what it was written to do: a hook must CITE a finding from its own run. It does not require that finding to be EVIDENCED. Those are different claims, and the gap between them is the difference between 'we noticed' and 'we checked'. I have NOT changed it. Tightening the guard to demand an evidence URL would invalidate all 40 existing hooks, which may well be the right answer, but it is a decision about how we open a conversation with a stranger and that is yours to make.

blockers.title: Production has drifted from the repository -- now measured exactly
blockers.meaning: This is no longer an estimate. Production holds 98 migrations; this repository holds 48. Fifty-four are applied in production and exist in no repository file; four are in the repository and have never been applied; sixteen more were applied under different version stamps than the files carry, which is the mechanical reason the protected one-click migration workflow cannot run. The number 0048 has been used by two unrelated migrations, so migration numbers no longer identify migrations. The important discovery: the fifty-four include the ENTIRE BarberOS product (eleven migrations, two schemas, twenty-four tables, fifty-four functions) plus two product lines nobody has documented -- dma_* (17 migrations, 28 tables) and jobscout_* (8 migrations, 8 tables) -- and one leftover object called temp_perftest_page_twin. None of it has a file, a test, a review or a rollback path. If that project were lost, nothing in this repository could rebuild it. Three questions only you can answer: where is the BarberOS application that calls those 17 RPCs (there is no client for them in source control); where did the 50 Western New York barbershop prospects come from (they were imported from a spreadsheet); and do the dma_* and jobscout_* lines still matter -- keep, export or retire? The fix is to bring the live schema back into source control as migrations that reproduce it exactly, with the pgTAP tests that should have come with them, applying nothing. That needs your go-ahead.
